explanations.answer: Not one will be left on another
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says, friend. He tells them, “…not one stone will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.” The disciples were busy admiring the stonework, and I bet nobody saw that sentence coming. It's a heavy word, and I think it landed hard.

explanations.answer: They will last a thousand years
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say anything about a thousand years. He says the time will come when not one stone is left on another. The stones are beautiful, but He says they won't stay standing. I think that's a hard thing to hear while you're still admiring them.

explanations.answer: They will all be covered in gold
explanations.explanation: Gold is a fun guess, friend, but Jesus says nothing like that. The disciples are talking about beautiful stones and consecrated gifts, and He says the time will come when not one stone is left on another. Every one will be thrown down. No gold shows up anywhere in His answer.

explanations.answer: When it will happen and what the sign will be
explanations.explanation: Two questions, just like you said. They ask, “when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that they are about to take place?” I think they want a heads up, and who wouldn't? Stay close, because Jesus answers with a warning instead of a date.

explanations.answer: Who will do it and how they can stop it
explanations.explanation: Nope, the disciples don't ask who or how to stop it. They ask, “when will these things happen? And what will be the sign that they are about to take place?” They want the timing and a warning sign. Asking how to stop it is a whole different question, friend.

explanations.answer: Why it must happen and where they should go
explanations.explanation: The disciples don't ask why, and they don't ask where to go. They call Him Teacher and ask when these things will happen and what the sign will be. I can see why the other questions might sound natural, though. If a building were about to come down, I'd want directions too.

Deceived is the word. Jesus says, “See to it that you are not deceived.” He warns that many will come in His name saying, “I am He…” and, “The time is near.” His answer is a caution before anything else, and He says, “Do not follow them.”

Discouraged is a fair guess after a hard word like that. But Jesus actually says, “See to it that you are not deceived.” The worry He names is about people who come in His name claiming, “I am He…” He's watching out for the disciples so they don't follow the wrong voices.

Delayed makes sense when you're asking about timing, friend. But Jesus says, “See to it that you are not deceived.” The warning is about many who will come in His name and say, “The time is near.” His instruction to the disciples about them is short: “Do not follow them.”

I can see why that sounds possible, but it's the other way around. Jesus says many will come in His name claiming, “I am He…” and, “The time is near.” Then He says, “Do not follow them.” So the answer is False, and His words are clear.

False is right. About the people who claim, “The time is near.” Jesus says, “Do not follow them.” He doesn't leave any wiggle room there. When someone shows up with a big announcement, the disciples are to hold on to what Jesus told them.

Do not be alarmed is what Jesus says. He says, “When you hear of wars and rebellions, do not be alarmed.” Now, I get alarmed when the oven light flickers, so this is a tall order. But He's the One saying it, and that matters.

Jesus doesn't send them off to fight. He says, “When you hear of wars and rebellions, do not be alarmed.” The instruction is about how they respond to the news, and He doesn't give them a battle to join. So the answer is the calm one, friend.

Jesus doesn't tell them to go into the temple and stay put. He says, “When you hear of wars and rebellions, do not be alarmed.” That's the whole instruction for hearing that news. I'd say it's worth hearing twice.

True. Jesus says, “These things must happen first, but the end is not imminent.” So wars and rebellions aren't a signal that everything is wrapping up right away. That's why He tells them not to be alarmed. The news can sound loud, but Jesus has already told them what to make of it.

It's True, friend, and that's easy to flip around. Jesus says, “These things must happen first, but the end is not imminent.” So wars and rebellions don't mean the end is coming right away. That's why He tells the disciples not to be alarmed.

That's the list. Jesus says, “There will be great earthquakes, famines, and pestilences in various places…” It's a heavy list, and He doesn't sugarcoat it. But He gave it to the disciples ahead of time, and I think that's a kindness.

Those are real troubles, friend, but they aren't on Jesus' list here. He says there will be great earthquakes, famines and pestilences in various places. Pestilences is an old word, and it's easy to skate past it. Those three are the ones to remember.

That sounds like a scary list, I'll give you that. But Jesus doesn't say locusts, hail or darkness here. He says, “There will be great earthquakes, famines, and pestilences in various places…” Those three are the ones to hold on to.

Signs is the word. Jesus says there will be “…fearful sights and great signs from heaven.” Remember that the disciples asked about a sign. Signs are part of His answer, though He also warns them about people claiming, “The time is near.” and says, “Do not follow them.” (Luke 21:8)

Storms is a good guess, since the sky is where we look. But Jesus says there will be “…fearful sights and great signs from heaven.” The word is signs. The disciples asked Him about a sign, so it fits that the word comes up.

Voices from heaven would be dramatic, wouldn't it? But Jesus says there will be “…fearful sights and great signs from heaven.” The word in the text is signs. He doesn't mention any voices in this list.

It's the other way around, friend. Jesus says, “But before all this, they will seize you and persecute you.” So the disciples face it before the earthquakes and signs, and it's not saved for the end of the list. It's a sobering word to hear, and He doesn't hide the order.

False is right. Jesus says, “But before all this, they will seize you and persecute you.” That means it comes first, before the wars and earthquakes and signs. He turns from the whole world to the people right in front of Him. That's the timing He gives them.

explanations.answer: A chance to serve as witnesses
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Jesus says, “This will be your opportunity to serve as witnesses.” Kings and governors sound like the end of the road to me. He calls it an opportunity. I think that's a big shift in how to look at it.

explanations.answer: A sign the end has come
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, but Jesus doesn't call it that. He says, “This will be your opportunity to serve as witnesses.” He's already told them the end is not imminent when they hear of wars. So He's describing a chance to witness, and He isn't calling it a sign.
Staying quiet isn't what He says. He calls it “…your opportunity to serve as witnesses.” A witness speaks about what they know. So Jesus describes the moment as a chance to do exactly that.

explanations.answer: Jesus will give them speech and wisdom
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, “For I will give you speech and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict.” So they don't have to write the speech beforehand. I'd still be tempted to practice in the mirror, but He's got it covered.

explanations.answer: The kings will be on their side
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't promise that the kings will be on their side. He says, “For I will give you speech and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict.” The help comes from Him. That's the reason they don't need to plan ahead.

explanations.answer: No one will ask them anything
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that, friend. He talks about adversaries and says He will give the disciples speech and wisdom that none of them will be able to resist or contradict. He tells them to make up their minds not to worry beforehand how to defend themselves. The words come from Him.

explanations.answer: Their parents and relatives and friends
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “You will be betrayed even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends…” That's a heavy part, and I think it hurts to hear. These are the people closest to them. Jesus doesn't hide it from the disciples.

Jesus doesn't name soldiers here. He says the disciples will be betrayed “…even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends…” The word even tells you these are people close to them. It's a heavy line, so I think it's worth taking slowly.

Servants and hired workers aren't on Jesus' list. He says, “You will be betrayed even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends…” Those are family and friends. It's a hard line, and I think it hurts to hear.

True. Right after the hard words, Jesus says, “Yet not even a hair of your head will perish.” That sits next to being hated and some being put to death. Those words come together in what He says to them.

It's True, friend, even though it sounds surprising here. Jesus says, “Yet not even a hair of your head will perish.” He says it right after warning that some will be put to death and that they will be hated by everyone. Those words come together in what He says to them.

That's right. Jesus says, “By your patient endurance you will gain your souls.” Patient endurance means sticking with it. That's about the opposite of what most of us want when something hard shows up.

Fighting back is a natural thought, but it's not what Jesus says. He says, “By your patient endurance you will gain your souls.” The key is patient endurance. That means sticking with it, and no fighting is mentioned.
Silence isn't the answer here. Jesus says, “By your patient endurance you will gain your souls.” And earlier He says He'll give them speech and wisdom. So silence isn't how He describes it.

That's the sign. Jesus says, “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near.” Notice He says you will know. The disciples asked for a sign earlier, and this is one He gives them.

explanations.answer: A new star over the city
explanations.explanation: A new star would be pretty to look at, but Jesus doesn't say that. He says, “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near.” The sign is armies around the city. It's a sober picture, friend.

Shutting doors is a creative guess, friend. But Jesus says the sign is seeing “…Jerusalem surrounded by armies…” That's when they will know her desolation is near. He gives them something they can see with their own eyes.

Mountains it is. Jesus says, “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains…” He tells them to leave, and He doesn't tell them to stay and wait it out. When Jesus says go, I think going is the move.

The temple is a natural guess, since it's the building they were just admiring. But Jesus says, “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains…” The direction is away from the city and toward the mountains. That's the instruction He gives.

Sea is a reasonable guess if you're picturing a getaway. But Jesus says, “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains…” He names the mountains. Heading to high ground is the direction in His words.

It's the opposite, friend. Jesus says, “…let those in the city get out, and let those in the country stay out of the city.” So people in the country don't come in. It might seem backwards, but it's what He says.

False is right. Jesus says, “…let those in the city get out, and let those in the country stay out of the city.” People in the city leave, and people in the country keep away from it. A city wall might look safe, but that's not the direction He gives.

explanations.answer: To fulfill all that is written
explanations.explanation: Right. Jesus says, “For these are the days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written.” That ties these days to what Scripture has already said. It's a heavy passage, friend. The purpose He names is fulfilling all that is written.

explanations.answer: To make the temple new again
explanations.explanation: That's not what Jesus says. He says these are the days of vengeance, “…to fulfill all that is written.” Earlier He told the disciples that every stone would be thrown down. A renewed temple isn't part of what He says here.

explanations.answer: To crown a new king there
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't mention crowning anyone. He says, “For these are the days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written.” The purpose He names is fulfilling what is written. It's a serious moment, friend.

Not quite, friend. Jesus says, “And Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.” The Gentiles are people from the nations. There's an until in that sentence, and forever isn't what He says.

False is right. Jesus says, “And Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.” That little word until matters. He doesn't say forever, and He isn't done talking yet.
